exercises.prompt: Daniela, in Guadalajara (Mexico), turns to her two best friends and asks where they're from. Which pronoun does she use for "you all"?
hints: She is in Latin America.
In Latin America one word covers every "you all", formal or informal.

options.label: ustedes
options.feedback: Yes. In Latin America *ustedes* is used for any group, friends included.

options.label: vosotros
options.feedback: Not yet — *vosotros* is the informal plural in most of Spain, not in Mexico.

options.label: ellos
options.feedback: Not yet — *ellos* means "they": she would be talking *about* her friends, not to them.

exercises.solution: **Ustedes.** Across Latin America, *ustedes* is the only plural "you", used with friends and strangers alike: *¿De dónde son ustedes?* A speaker from most of Spain would say *vosotros* to friends: *¿De dónde sois?*

exercises.prompt: Fill the gap with the right form of **ser**: *Nosotros ___ de Chile.* (Type only the missing word.)
hints: *Nosotros* is "we".
The "we" form of *ser* ends in -mos.

feedback.message: Almost — *son* is "they are" or "you all are". For "we are", use *somos*.

exercises.solution: **somos**: *Nosotros somos de Chile* (We are from Chile). The full present of *ser*: *soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son*.

exercises.prompt: Fill the gap with the right form of **ser**: *Ellas ___ médicas.* (Type only the missing word.)
hints: *Ellas* means "they" (all female).
It's the same form as for *ustedes*.

feedback.message: Almost — *es* is singular (he, she, you formal). *Ellas* is plural, so use *son*.

exercises.solution: **son**: *Ellas son médicas* (They are doctors). *Ellos, ellas* and *ustedes* all share the form *son*. Notice that *médicas* agrees with *ellas*: feminine and plural.

hints: Use *ser* + *de* + the country.
The "I" form of *ser* is *soy*. *México* has an accent.

feedback.message: Not yet — origin uses *ser*, not *estar*: *Soy de México*.
Almost — "from" a place is just *de*: *Soy de México*.

exercises.solution: **Soy de México** (or *Yo soy de México*, with emphasis on "I"). Origin takes *ser* + *de*. Remember the *x* in *México* sounds like the Spanish *j*: "MEH-hee-koh".

exercises.prompt: Lucía is from Spain. Complete: *Lucía es ___.* (Type only the nationality.)
hints: The masculine form is *español*, which ends in a consonant.
For a consonant ending, add -a for the feminine. Use a small letter.

feedback.message: Almost — *español* is masculine. Lucía is a woman, so add -a: *española*.
Not yet — *España* is the country. The nationality is *español*, *española*.

exercises.solution: **española.** Nationalities ending in a consonant add -a in the feminine: *español → española*, *inglés → inglesa*, *alemán → alemana*. And unlike English, Spanish writes nationalities with a small letter.

hints: Use *ser*: the form for *ella* is *es*.
With a bare profession after *ser*, Spanish leaves out "a". The profession agrees with her: *enfermera*.

feedback.message: Almost — with a bare profession after *ser*, Spanish drops the article: *Es enfermera*.
Almost — with a bare profession after *ser*, Spanish drops the article: *Ella es enfermera*.
Almost — *enfermero* is a male nurse. For "she", use *enfermera*.
Almost — *enfermero* is a male nurse. For "she", use *enfermera*.

exercises.solution: **Es enfermera** (or *Ella es enfermera*). Three things happen: *ser* in the *ella* form (*es*), the feminine profession (*enfermera*), and **no article** before a bare profession, unlike English "a nurse".

exercises.prompt: Which of these nouns are **masculine**? Choose all that apply.
hints: Some very common nouns break the -o / -a pattern.
Two of these end in -a but are masculine; one ends in -o but is feminine.

options.label: día (day)
options.feedback: Yes: *el día*, an exception to the -a pattern.

options.label: mano (hand)
options.feedback: Not this one — *la mano* is feminine, despite the -o.

options.label: ciudad (city)
options.feedback: Not this one — words in -dad are feminine: *la ciudad*.

exercises.solution: **el día** and **el mapa** are masculine, although they end in -a; **la mano** is feminine although it ends in -o; and **la ciudad** is feminine, as are all nouns ending in -dad. This is why it pays to learn each noun with its article.

exercises.prompt: Make this plural: *el profesor inglés* (the English teacher) → ___
hints: All three words change: the article, the noun and the nationality.
Words ending in a consonant add -es. Check whether *ingleses* still needs its accent.

feedback.message: Almost — *ingleses* ends in -s and is stressed on the second-to-last syllable, so it needs no written accent.
Almost — *profesores* is masculine, so the article is *los*.

exercises.solution: **los profesores ingleses.** *el → los*; *profesor* ends in a consonant, so *-es*: *profesores*; *inglés* also adds *-es*, and the written accent disappears because *ingleses* (in-GLE-ses) now follows the normal stress rule.

hints: Put *no* directly before the verb.
"We are" is *somos*; *estudiante* has one form for men and women, and its plural adds -s.

feedback.message: Almost — *no* goes before the verb: *No somos estudiantes*.
Almost — that would be "We aren't *the* students". With a bare profession or role after *ser*, leave out the article.

exercises.solution: **No somos estudiantes** (or *Nosotros/Nosotras no somos estudiantes*). *No* goes immediately before the verb, and there is no article before *estudiantes*.

exercises.prompt: Ask an older stranger, politely: **Where are you from?**
hints: Use *usted*, which takes the same verb form as *él* and *ella*.
The preposition goes first: *¿De dónde…?*

feedback.message: That's the informal question, with *tú*. With an older stranger, use *usted*: *¿De dónde es usted?*
Almost — Spanish never puts the preposition at the end. It goes first: *¿De dónde es usted?*

exercises.solution: **¿De dónde es usted?** *Usted* takes the third-person form *es*, and *de* comes at the start of the question, never at the end as in English "Where are you from?". *Dónde* has an accent because it is a question word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct for "They (two women) are Canadian"?
hints: Check three things: the verb, the ending of the nationality, and the capital letter.
Nationalities ending in -e don't change for gender.

options.label: Ellas son canadienses.
options.feedback: Yes: plural verb, -e nationality with only -s added, small letter.

options.label: Ellas son canadiensas.
options.feedback: Not yet — *canadiense* ends in -e and has the same form for men and women; the plural just adds -s.

options.label: Ellas son Canadienses.
options.feedback: Not yet — in Spanish, nationalities take a small letter.

exercises.solution: **Ellas son canadienses.** *Ellas* takes *son*; *canadiense* ends in -e, so it is the same for men and women and only adds -s in the plural; and nationalities are not capitalised in Spanish.

exercises.prompt: A classmate asks *¿Eres de Argentina?* You're not. Which answer is natural and correct?
hints: *No* goes right before the verb.
It's normal to say *no* twice: once as the answer, once to make the verb negative.

options.label: No, no soy de Argentina.
options.feedback: Yes: the first *no* answers the question, the second negates *soy*.

options.label: No, soy no de Argentina.
options.feedback: Not yet — *no* goes before the verb, not after it.

options.label: No, no eres de Argentina.
options.feedback: Not yet — *eres* means "you are". Answering about yourself, use *soy*.

exercises.solution: **No, no soy de Argentina.** The first *no* is the answer; the second, placed right before the verb, makes the sentence negative. The question used *eres* (you are), so the answer switches to *soy* (I am).
